newsitem.title: CONGO: Zaire's Mobutu fails to negotiate dignified exit.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu fails to negotiate dignified exit.

text.p: Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko failed to negotiate a dignified exit during talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila on a South African ship on Sunday.
Kabila said his forces, reported by residents to be within 100 km (60 miles) of Kinshasa and advancing, would fight on while Mobutu considered his demand that he resign.
A statement issued at the end of a face-to-face meeting on board the customised icebreaker SAS Outeniqua said that Mobutu had offered to hand power to an elected successor.
But the civil war rivals failed to agree on the terms of Mobutu's departure.

South African President Nelson Mandela, who hosted the meeting, told a closing news conference that he would convene a fresh round of talks in eight to 10 days to "narrow the gap between the two parties".
Residents, contacted from Kinshasa, said rebels advancing rapidly in trucks were under 100 km (60 miles) of the capital, well within striking distance. The city itself was calm.

"I made it clear a ceasefire is out of the question and my forces will continue to advance on all fronts. If we make it to Kinshasa before the eight days then too bad but we cannot wait while he makes up his mind," Kabila told Reuters by telephone from the ship in Congo's port of Pointe Noire.
In northeastern Zaire, over 100 Rwandan Hutu refugees suffocated or were crushed to death on Sunday in a train carrying them from a refugee camp to be repatriated by air.
Aid workers and journalists saw dozens of bodies of refugees tumbling from open railway carriages as the train pulled into the station in the rebel-held city of Kisangani.
Aboard the South African ship, U.N. and Organisation of African Unity special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, reading the final statement, said Mobutu had offered to stand down.
Kabila, for his part, insisted that his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire should act as the transitional authority to organise elections, he added.
Witnesses said Mobutu left the ship immediately after the closing news conference. His destination was unclear. Kabila set off for his Lubumbashi headquarters, officials in Angola said.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated the sprawling yet mineral-rich nation at the heart of Africa for more than three decades.

He was among a handful of world leaders such as the late Shah of Iran, the late President Ferdinand Marcos of the Philippines and Chile's Augusto Pinochet who were propped up by the United States as bulwarks against Soviet communism.
Battling cancer and the whirlwind revolt at home, he looked grim-faced and sad as he boarded the SAS Outeniqua where Kabila and Mandela had been waiting for him since late Saturday.
Kabila, 56, looked relaxed and smiled broadly as he entered the closing news conference.
His forces, who took up arms in October, control three quarters of the sprawling nation at the heart of Africa.
One diplomat said the rebel leader had been looking for any excuse not to come. At one point, a frustrated Mandela got on the satellite phone to him in Angola and shouted down the line.
Mobutu, wearing his trade-mark leopard-skin hat, boarded the ship with difficulty on Friday, when talks were first planned. Unable to climb 31 steps, he was driven on board up a ramp.

On Sunday, he and his wife Bobi Ladawa squeezed into a makeshift quayside lift and were hoisted on board. Mobutu clutched Bobi Ladawa's hand. In his other hand he gripped his usual carved walking stick.

Zaire accuses Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of fighting alongside Kabila's forces. Independent sources say rebels have captured Mobutu's Lisala birthplace and are marching on Kinshasa and his jungle palace in Gbadolite in the north.
The military governor of Kinshasa urged residents to stay calm in the face of the rebel advance and told security forces to protect its population without discrimination.
The U.S. State Department urged American citizens to leave Zaire and warned them not to travel there, citing the "deteriorating security and political situation".
The United States, France, former colonial power Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
